title: SDK integration walkthrough - CrestPay
summary: Intro + quick overview of Redwood API/Console/Optimize, deep dive on Python/TypeScript SDKs, auth and env setup, quickstart example. Customer concerned about VPC/private deployment, latency and cost. Agreed to run a 2-week pilot with a small benchmark and follow up security docs.
next_steps: Redwood to send security questionnaire + SOC2 docs (Maya)
SE to share sample SDK repo and quickstart snippets (Diego)
Customer to provision test dataset and share perf target (Liam)
Schedule pilot kickoff meeting week of 2025-09-29
action_items: Maya - send SOC2 + security pack by 2025-09-19
Diego - push example repo with Python + TS quickstarts to GitHub by 2025-09-20
Liam - confirm baseline traffic patterns and perf targets by 2025-09-24
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-09-18 16:00 PDT | Duration: 42 mins
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramirez (Redwood SE), Priya Anand (Redwood SRE); Liam O'Connor (CrestPay Lead Eng), Nina Patel (Product), Harold King (CTO), Sam (Engineer)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, really quick agenda - we'll do a short product overview then jump into SDK integration in Python and TypeScript, auth, env setup and a quickstart. please mute if not speaking.
[00:12] Liam: Yep thanks, excited. Our main goals are getting a low-friction SDK integration and figuring out how to run in our VPC for compliance.
[00:20] Maya: Totally, that's exactly what Diego and Priya will cover. Diego do you want to do a 5 minute API/Console overview?
[00:28] Diego: Sure, quick high-level: Redwood exposes text gen, chat, embeddings via a simple REST/SDK. Console shows per-route cost, latency dashboards, and Optimize gives recommendations for batching and quantization. sorry typo, quant -- quant profiles.
[00:45] Harold: Quick Q - do we need to change our auth flow for SSO? We currently use Okta and short-lived tokens.
[00:52] Priya: We support API keys and we also have SAML SSO for the console. For private deployments we can integrate with customer KMS and SSO via SAML/SCIM. There are some extra steps for on-prem but it's supported.
[01:05] Nina: Are there RBAC roles per route? We need limited access for support engineers.
[01:10] Diego: Yes, in Console you can set role-based access, and token scopes can be limited per route. We usually recommend service tokens for backend calls and scoped user tokens for user-initiated actions.
[01:24] Maya: Ok now SDK deep dive -- Diego?
[01:28] Diego: Alright, I'll share screen -- (screen share noise) -- jumping into the Python quickstart. Basic install pip install redwood-inference (note: package name in prerelease may differ). Typical code: import redwood; client = redwood.Client(api_key=os.getenv("REDWOOD_API_KEY")); resp = client.generate(model="redwood-7b", prompt="hello"); print(resp.text)
[01:58] Sam: Does the SDK handle streaming? We have a chat UI that needs token-level streaming.
[02:05] Diego: Yes, both Python and TS SDKs support streaming via event callbacks or async iterators. Example in TS: const stream = client.stream.generate(...); for await (const chunk of stream) { updateUI(chunk) } -- sorry chat, for await syntax in Node.
[02:20] Liam: Any gotchas with Node envs vs serverless? We run in AWS Lambda and Vercel for some microservices.
[02:28] Diego: For serverless, we recommend shorter-lived clients and connection pooling considerations. Also for streaming on edge platforms, use the SDK over HTTP streaming where possible - there is a small cold-start memory overhead if you initialize heavy clients each request.
[02:44] Nina: How does auth work in the SDK? We prefer not to store long-lived keys in repo.
[02:50] Diego: We encourage using environment variables injected at deploy time, or AWS Secret Manager/SSM to fetch keys. For Dedicated or Private, you can wire up internal token minting via our token exchange endpoint or service tokens with limited TTLs. That's also in the quickstart repo.
[03:10] Harold: We're asking about VPC/private: network egress and data residency are critical. What are the steps for private deployment?
[03:20] Priya: For Private we ship a control plane and a private runtime that can sit in your VPC or on-prem. You get customer managed networking, KMS integration for keys, and audit logs. There is a deploy checklist: infra sizing, GPU selection, and firewall rules. We typically run a short discovery then a pilot deploy.
[03:43] Liam: Any performance numbers for gen latency at 8k context?
[03:47] Diego: Latency varies a lot by model, sequence length, and hardware. For a 7B on A100 and 2k avg sequence we see median token latency ~15-30ms per token with batching; at 8k it increases - but Optimize can suggest KV caching and batching policies to hit your SLOs. These are roughs, we'd run a bench on your workload.
[04:10] Sam: Can we run local benchmarks with the SDK?
[04:14] Diego: Yes, the SDK includes a bench harness and we can share a script to run against hosted or dedicated endpoints. We'll add a small sample dataset for common ecommerce chat flows.
[04:26] Maya: Let's walk through a demo quickstart - Diego take the Python flow and then TS.
[04:30] Diego: Python quickstart: 1) pip install redwood-inference; 2) export REDWOOD_API_KEY=xxx; 3) run python quickstart.py which calls client.generate and streams. The quickstart includes example of file-based prompts, embedding calls, and using the Console to view per-route metrics.
[05:00] (short pause as Diego pastes code)
[05:12] Diego: TypeScript quickstart: npm i @redwood/inference; set env NEXT_PUBLIC_REDWOOD_API_KEY for frontend or REDWOOD_API_KEY for server; example uses server route to proxy requests so keys are never exposed in client-side bundle.
[05:30] Nina: That's helpful - we want to ensure our frontend cannot leak keys. The server-proxy pattern is what we have today.
[05:36] Diego: Right, recommended pattern. Also you can use function-to-function auth: our short-lived tokens for client sessions so UI can call your backend exchange for ephemeral keys.
[05:48] Liam: Any reference code for the proxy pattern?
[05:51] Diego: I'll put that in the repo. The sample includes Lambda, Vercel, and Next.js examples.
[05:58] Maya: Quick demo of Console. (screen share) You can see per-route latency, token cost breakdown, and Optimize suggestions. Note the rollout controls for canary and automatic fallback to a cheaper model if latency spikes.
[06:20] Harold: About fallbacks - are those transparent to the client? We need consistent outputs.
[06:26] Priya: Fallbacks are policy-driven. You can set rollouts to use compatible model variants and we emit logs/traces in Console for each fallback so you can track regressions. For strict consistency you can pin a model version and disable fallbacks.
[06:45] Sam: Our use case is a customer support assistant with moderate throughput. Cost is a big driver. Does Optimize automatically suggest quantization?
[06:53] Diego: Optimize gives recommendations based on your workload - quantization profiles, batching windows, and cache policies. It can also suggest cheaper model variants and estimate cost per 1M tokens.
[07:07] Nina: What's the onboarding time for Dedicated? We have a Q4 timeline and want to start pilot in October.
[07:12] Maya: Dedicated typically 4-8 weeks depending on infra procurement; Private longer. For pilot we can start with hosted API or a small Dedicated pool. Goal would be pilot kickoff last week of Sept/first week Oct, which matches your Q4 plans.
[07:28] Liam: Ok let's talk about a small benchmark - our perf target is p95 tail latency for chat under 500ms and cost lower than $X per 1K messages - we'll share exact numbers.
[07:40] Diego: We'll run a benchmark using your prompt sets. Typical next step is we send the bench harness and you run against hosted endpoint (or we run in our test tenant) and we iterate.
[07:55] Maya: Are there any legal or procurement blockers up front?
[07:58] Harold: We'll need SOC2, data processing addendum and standard security questionnaire - legal will only sign after SI review.
[08:07] Maya: We'll send SOC2 and security pack today, plus DPA template.
[08:12] (brief cross talk)
[08:20] Diego: Back to SDK details - error handling: SDK surfaces structured errors and retry helpers. For rate limits we recommend using token-based quotas per route; the SDK has a retry policy you can configure. Also we support idempotency keys for non-deterministic ops.
[08:42] Sam: What about streaming over SSE vs websockets?
[08:46] Diego: Both supported. For browsers we typically use EventSource/SSE, for node native websockets or HTTP2 streams. The quickstart includes SSE client code for Chromium-based browsers.
[09:05] Nina: Any gotchas with TypeScript types? Are they well typed?
[09:09] Diego: Types are included; there's an ongoing issue where some edge-case model params types are slightly off but it is fast-evolving. We'll include a pinned version that works with your stack.
[09:22] Liam: Security: KMS integration - can Redwood use our AWS KMS for key wrap?
[09:27] Priya: Yes, for Private and Dedicated we can integrate your KMS; for hosted we support customer-managed keys via BYOK flows for sensitive keys. We'll share the KMS integration doc.
[09:39] Maya: Let's capture concrete next steps.
[09:42] Nina: I'll own scheduling pilot kickoff with internal stakeholders.
[09:45] Maya: Great - action items to recap in follow up email.
[09:50] Harold: One more question - is there any prework our infra team needs before pilot?
[09:54] Priya: If you want private networking, we need firewall rules, subnet setup and EKS/VM sizing. We'll send a checklist. For hosted pilot, none required beyond API keys and sample traffic.
[10:10] Maya: Thanks everyone - we'll send the repo, SOC2, and bench harness. Next call: pilot kickoff week of Sep 29.
[10:20] Liam: Thanks - appreciate the walkthrough.
[10:25] (meeting ends)
notes: Redwood to share quickstart repo with Python & TypeScript examples
Customer requests SOC2/DPA and security questionnaire
